pr_title: Add additional Delaying Queue methods which enable finer control over the delaying and de-duplication features
pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

A delaying queue is best thought of as an **'active'** queue coupled with a **'waiting'** queue where items can sit out a length of time before they automatically mature out of **'waiting'** and into the **'active'** queue part.  They are most often used by controllers wanting to remember to retry something that failed.

This PR offers the following benefits:

* Preserves original `Add()` and `AddAfter()` behaviour in order to support existing clients without surprises.
* New behaviours in the `DelayingInterface` which allow finer control of queuing:
  * `AddWithOptions()` that allows clients finer control over the queueing behaviour.
  * `DoneWaiting()` so a client can remove an item from the **'waiting'** queue.
  * `IsWaiting()` reports back if an item is in the **'waiting'** queue.
  * `LenWaiting()` reports the length of the **'waiting'** queue.
* A new method in the **'active'** queue `Interface`: 
  *   `IsQueued()` reports back if an item is in the **'active'** queue.

`AddWithOptions()` is asynchronous and will often return back to the client faster than calling `Add()` or `AddAfter()`.

For existing clients, calling `Add()` and `AddAfter()` will continue to work exactly as before, but if a client moves to using `AddWithOptions()` - they can then control features which enable/disable deduplication of items between the "active" and "waiting" queue, where the item is already waiting choose which delay you want to use (the shortest, longest, existing, incoming).

All clients can now ask the DelayingQueue whether a specific item is in the "waiting" queue with `IsWaiting()` whether an item is queued in the "active" queue with `IsQueued()`.  To get the length of the "waiting" queue they can call `LenWaiting()` and for the "active" queue `Len()` (which is an existing implementation).

It is already possible to forget an item from the "active" queue by calling the method `Done()`.  This PR adds a corresponding feature for the "waiting" queue by calling `DoneWaiting()`.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

Fixes #112325
Fixes #110642

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
NONE
```

Instead of making this a construction setting (which adds a lot of complexity and constrains all callers to doing the same thing), I would do this:

* Override the Add method (as you have done) and make it do what you called "promote" (I think you are right that the current behavior is surprising)
* Add an `AddOutOfBand` method and make it do what you called "ignore" (pass through to underlying queue)
* Add an `AddIfNotDelaying` method to support the last mode.

I think @deads2k should sign off on this

Hi @lavalamp thanks for taking a look!  Whilst it would be nice in some ways to implement this through new methods I think that this needs to be a constructor setting for the following reasons:
* We need to adjust the immediate add behaviour of both the immediate Add() being called by the client controller (which could be done through different methods as you suggest) but we also need to be able to adjust the immediate add behaviour when an item is popped out of the waiting channel in the waitingLoop() (when the clock has advanced past the delay time).  Both type of immediate adds need to be handled the same way so we need somewhere to store and look up which behaviour to use.
* They way I have implemented it (with the constructor option) allows a client of the package to change the queue behaviour by changing a single line of code (the call to create the queue).  We can change the behaviour without needing to review the controllers choices of Add() methods.  This makes it easier for clients of the package and allows us to change the default behaviour (like I am for rate limiters) without requiring any changes to clients.
* I'm would worry about someone doing something funky like trying to use multiple of the different Add behaviour functions against the same delayed queue because it will be very easy to get surprising behaviour with unintended consequences.  I'd rather the queue has a set behaviour and a really simple immediate add interface Add() rather than relying on the client to work out their own complex behaviour (someone might be able to do something genius, but lots of other people may trip up over what they are trying to achieve).

> we also need to be able to adjust the immediate add behaviour when an item is popped out of the waiting channel in the waitingLoop() (when the clock has advanced past the delay time)

Why would anyone want something other than the "promote" behavior for this? (I didn't read the entire diff)

In general we should *not* give people a choice like this without an extremely good reason.

> They way I have implemented it (with the constructor option) allows a client of the package to change the queue behaviour by changing a single line of code (the call to create the queue).

But my suggestion of changing the default fixes it for ~everyone just by recompiling! I think probably no one wants the current behavior?

> someone doing something funky like trying to use multiple of the different Add behaviour functions against the same delayed queue because it will be very easy to get surprising behaviour with unintended consequences

Sure, I'd be fine with actually not allowing the pass-through option at all (edit: maybe? I have to think more?). But in general I think the person making a call to Add is in the best position to decide what this should do to pending calls for the same thing if it's already in the queue.

Thanks!  A few more thoughts... open to more helpful suggestions!

> Why would anyone want something other than the "promote" behavior for this? (I didn't read the entire diff)

Maybe the devil is in the detail here but I do think that we should be consistent in the queue behaviour whether receiving an immediate add() from a client or popping off a delayed item from the waiting channel that due for an immediate add().  For example, if I decide I want a delaying queue with AddBlockedByWaiting behaviour in order to better adhere to the rate limiter - it would break this intention if when performing immediate adds from within the waitingLoop() to default to the "promote" behaviour, which pre-empts the rate-limit each time.

I *could* remove the original behaviour entirely if that's preferable?!  That would leave us we two different useful behaviours - 1) Promote waiting items when adding (make the new default), and 2 - block immediate adds when waiting (Strict) so that failures properly adhere to the rate-limited exponential backoff and can not be pre-empted.

> But my suggestion of changing the default fixes it for ~everyone just by recompiling! I think probably no one wants the current behaviour?

Yeah I was being more cautious and only changing the default for all RateLimited Queues for everyone just by compiling and not all delaying queues everywhere.  Personally, I don't think the original behaviour is something worth keeping but I don't want to introduce a change that breaks some obscure use of the delaying queue functionality that I'm not aware of. happy to be steered here, and happy to remove the original behaviour and make the promote method default for all.  I still want the choice of a stricter pattern to be specifically requested where useful (like in the AvailableConditionController) so it is worth supporting the choosing the required behaviour of the queue upon construction.

> But in general I think the person making a call to Add is in the best position to decide what this should do to pending calls for the same thing if it's already in the queue

Yes, and that is generally the same person that has decided upon the queue type they need.  I guess what I'm saying, is that as of yet I can't think of a use-case where allowing mixed behaviours is good to offset my concern about someone misusing the wrong method or both methods without appreciating the consequences.
Another option would be to drop the strict mode altogether so we just keep the "promotes" behaviour as default but that would be shame as I already have a use-case for the stricter behaviour.

I think it is better to think of the delaying/rate-limiting as a tool to help you hit a target, and not as a cop to guarantee you don't exceed the target. It clearly works that way today, and I think it's best to keep it that way.

I think it is reasonable for people calling Add to decide whether they're making sure the thing is the queue, or adding it now (removing it from the queue). We can document that only the former choice obeys the rate limit in all cases.

The current behavior of having duplicate calls is at least 90% bug IMO. Maybe @deads2k recalls some reason for it to work this way?

Many thanks for your comments @lavalamp!  I've updated the PR to make the "promote" behaviour the default and remove the options from the constructor.  I have attempted to preserve the ability to support both "preemptable" and "non-preemptable" behaviours so that the PR still provides solutions for both of the behaviours that I have highlighted in the issue.
/cc @deads2k

Hi, I would have gone for additional methods, but for the following two reasons: -
* The immediate Add() is presently initiated 3 different ways on a DelayingQueue:
  1. Via a direct client call to Add() on the underlying Interface (easy to create new methods with modified behaviour like you suggest)
  2. Client calls AddAfter() with a 0 duration (how would they set the desired behaviour of the subsequent Add() if there is more than one choice of behaviour option or method?)
  3. The client calls AddAfter() with a short duration and places the item in the waitingForAddCh but when the waitingLoop() receives the item from the channel, the wait time has already been reached, so instead of adding the item to the heap, it runs an immediate Add() (how can we choose the correct behaviour for this add unless we define it on the queue?). https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/661899f1a14680840e06c84bc3ff46f73d203012/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/workqueue/delaying_queue.go#L247-L257
* All of the existing client implementations of Delaying Queues and RateLimiting queues are unaware of any new functionality and will need modification to take advantage of the alternative behaviours.  Allowing the behaviour to be set consistently for the queue at construction is a single line change (and 0 line change for improved default behaviour).
  
I hope this helps?  The main reason for saving the type of immediate add behaviour we want to the queue at construction is for the consistency of handling the 3 immediate add cases so that we can make a consistent choice compatible with the desired behaviour of the queue.  I believe the behaviour needs to be set at construction in order to achieve this consistency and give the waitingLoop(), AddAfter() somewhere to go look up which type of immediate add to perform.

I can't yet picture a use-case for where a queue will be simultaneously preemptable (allow immediate adds) and non-preemptable (block immediate adds when the item is waiting).  I guess for the non-preemptable we could provide an additional method that allows a forced preemption for the client to call directly, but we wouldn't be able to support this function through AddAfter() or immediate Adds() coming out of the waitingForAddCh.

Would you prefer it if the add behaviour is somehow passed with each Add or AddAfter call from the client and saved with the queued item in its WaitFor so that each the desired behaviour can be set per queued item?  This could get pretty messy as we can't add extra parameters to Add() or AddAfter() without breaking existing clients?

Hmm @lavalamp maybe I could make it so AddAfter() and waitingLoop() always perform a preempting add (I.e an Interface Add() and removal from waiting heap) but have an extra method for AddUnlessWaiting() which does nothing if the item is already waiting.

Perhaps I got too hung up on ensuring consistent behavior across Add(), AddAfter() and inside waitingLoop()!  After all, people don’t typically call AddAfter() except for after an error do they?  So someone wanting stricter rate limiting would call AddUnlessWaiting() in place of Add() and AddAfter() after errors (as before).

No worries! (and sorry if this is outdated, I think you wrote a few messages while I was writing this)

Correct me if I'm wrong -- we only keep one copy of something in the waiting queue, we don't use this for calendaring (scheduling multiple adds in advance). So:
* `AddAfter(,0)` should always act like promote, or something is wrong, no? It would be extremely surprising if AddAfter(,0) added a long delay, no matter how the queue behaved otherwise. The point of the heap is to be able to take the earliest value, right?
* `AddAfter` with a short enough duration should also essentially be promote, right?

I agree AddAfter with 0 should accomplish the same thing as AddAfter with a short non-zero delay.

The one that is confusing is just plain old Add. Today it always means "ignore the queue and do something out of band". If we make it mean "promote" then actually it'll mean "delete any queue item and do it now". If instead we make it mean "wait", it'll effectively mean "do it later if it's in the queue, now otherwise". I guess I think we should make Add mean promote, because that's most similar to today's behavior, and because it'll be predictable. We could add a "AddIfNotWaiting" method for the other behavior?

Just to make sure I'm on the same page:
1) If Add(x) wins then x is immediately queued on active queue, followed by AddAfter(x, 1s) which will put it on the waiting queue to be popped off again in 1s for a second run.
2) If AddAfter(x, 1s) wins it gets placed on the waiting queue, immediately followed by Add(x) which will delete it from the waiting queue and add it to the active queue.

In Scenario 2, `x` I feel it makes sense that the immediate add squashes the delayed wait - which is what this PR is about.

Scenario 1 looks a bit messier!  Because Add(x) and AddAfter(x, 1s) are not destined for the same actual queue data structure (active vs waiting queue) these methods do not usually race at the time of calling, but when a delayed item is popped from the waiting queue it will be dropped if the same item is already in the active queue.  I agree that this does feel a bit more consistent but, I think, less well behaved because of them operating as two queues rather than one.

Perhaps we could make the new behaviour more consistent if we perform the same kind of collision for AddAfter() as we do for Add() - maybe if item 'x' is in the active queue when AddAfter() is called the delayed add should just be dropped?  My reasoning for this is that the request to add with the delay has found that another retry is already just about to happen anyway (and if that retry fails it will be retried with the delay again).  Will need to look at the code.

Hi @lavalamp 

What do you think about this idea?  In order to reduce the difference between performing racing Add()'s and AddAfter()'s how about we make AddAfter() collide with the active queue just like Add() does?  If AddAfter() drops the item if it is already actively queued then both Scenario 1 and Scenario 2 would result in a single execution.  My reasoning behind being able to drop an AddAfter(x, d) is that the delay always appears to be used for retries and delaying a retry when we are about to run the item again does not make sense, because x is about to execute again anyway and if that fails it will be retried (there's no need of the extra one and it would be more appropriate to compute a new delay than have the next execution happen earlier than the rate limiter defined).

I've tried this out in the commit above and quite like it but it has meant exposing a new method on the Active queue 'Interface': -
```
IsQueued(x interface{}) bool
```
This is so AddAfter() of the delaying queue is able to check if the item is already actively queued.
I quite like this because it adds another small efficiency gain and now we have:
* Dropping a delayed/waiting item when they are then immediately added with Add().
* Dropping a delayed item when it is already actively queued when calling AddAfter().

My fear would be that if someone wanted to pro-actively schedule a delayed item with AddAfter() and not expect it to be dropped because of an identical item in the active queue, however, attempting to use the delayingQueue for future scheduling may not be what they want either because of the fact that there is only ever one instance of an item in waiting and subsequent AddAfter()'s will be dropped or shorten the waiting time of the existing item.

What do you think?

I don't think I'd add a method like "IsQueued" since it's hard to use such a thing without locking.

My only point was that the special case wasn't needed any more and it'd be cleaner to get rid of it. I think?

I think there inherently is a race and that's OK, the only way to actually resolve it is to keep track of things that have "just been executed" and ignore requests that come just after that. But I don't think we should do that!

Hi @lavalamp - I quite like it, I can remove it but I'd like you to take another look, and then if you still feel it is better to remove it I can unwind my last commit.

You mention that it needs locking, and indeed it has it inside of the IsQueued method, the same as the other methods on the base queue.  Looking at the code I don't see anywhere where we are overlapping any locks which would cause deadlock, you'll notice that AddAfter does not lock anything itself and locks in sequence, i.e. first the lock on the underlying queue in order to report the IsQueued result, and then the lock on the waiting queue if the duration is 0 and needs to do an immediate add (with remove from waiting if queued).

What I like about testing for a collide with the active queue is that this does make the behaviour of the delaying queue act a bit more like a single queue, and I like the logical reasoning of "dropping a delayed add of 'x', where we know that there will be another processing of 'x' imminently" which is exactly what happens if you try to perform an Add() when 'x' is already in the active queue.  I like this, it solves the extra superfluous check if Add() and AddAfter() race but Add() wins.

I'll try and explain the race a little better now.  The race only affects testing because it is only in testing that we have a clock that doesn't automatically tick.  If we tick the fake clock forwards before an item has been processed and the nextReadyAt timer has been recalculated then because the calculation of the nextReadyAt timer is dependent on the clock.Now() the timer can be set for the stepped forward time + duration and not the original time.  Remembering that a synchronous call is only synchronous to the return of processArrivingEntry() and so if we write:

```
        q.AddWithOptions(second, DelayingOptions{Duration: 5 * time.Second, synchronous: true})
        fakeClock.Step(10 * time.Second)
	if err := waitForAdded(q, 1); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("expected success, got: %v", err)
	}
```

* The **AddWithOptions()** is going to return as soon as processArrivingEntry() finishes adding the option.
* The Step forward 10 seconds can occur **before** the waitingLoop has looped back around and recalculated the new nextReadyAt.
* The nextReadyAt is then calculated from the time stepped forward by 10 seconds + 5 seconds delay.
* The test will then usually timeout on a the **waitForAdded()** because nothing is going to step the clock forward again.

This is the race and one that I only discovered by adding the detailed logging.  In a nutshell, all of the testing does depend on synchronous calls and only by moving the update of nextReadyAt inside of **processArrivingEntry()** can we ensure that the nextReadyAt timer is updated before the synchronous return on the add (making it safe for the test to proceed stepping the clock forward).

I moved the re-calculation of the nextReadyAt time inside those routines that are capable of causing the head of the 'waiting' queue to change which is only two places:

*  when the waiting loop pops off ready items
*  when an item is added to or removed from the 'waiting' queue

The original implementation recalculates it every time through the loop, which I think is way too often.  For example, we don't need to recalculate it when an item is added to the waiting queue unless the new item was added to the front of the queue.  We don't need to recalculate it if an item is removed unless that item was the at the front of the queue.

If I move the logic back into the loop of the waiting loop then there was always be a race possible between the item being processed into the 'waiting' queue and the nextReadyAt being updated.  For that reason, nextReadyAt **must** be updated **before** processArrivingEntry() returns.  I've tried to mitigate this by only updating it when it is absolutely required - otherwise it would be being performed for every add.  It's not doing that now, it's only doing it when the item is the new top of the queue.

issue_context.title: delaying queue does not suppress duplicates between FIFO and waiting items
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/master/util/workqueue/delaying_queue.go suppresses duplicates within the FIFO, and suppresses duplicates within the priority queue of waiting items, but does not suppress duplicates between them.

### What did you expect to happen?

By the same logic that motivates duplicate suppression _within_ each of those two sections, there should also be duplicate suppression _between_ those two sections.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

@kubernetes/sig-api-machinery-misc 
@aojea

The scenario I've seen this is with the endpoint slice controller (xref https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/110639)
1. endpoint slice controller sync Service X
2. endpoint slice controller fails to reconcile Service X by reasons, it returns an error, requeue the Service and retry applying a backoff 
3. however, events related to Service X keep coming and new syncs of Service X are not delayed, only general rate limit of the queue apply but not the backoffs
/triage accepted

An item from the priority queue is put into the FIFO queue when the item's priority is reached i.e. item's wait period expired. The item is discarded by the FIFO queue if it is already present in the queue.

Here is the place where the item is discarded if a duplicate is present.

https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/master/util/workqueue/queue.go#L126


@MikeSpreitzer Can you please elaborate on the issue?

The issue is that because we write level-based controllers rather than edge-based ones, we never need two or more copies of an item in a queue; whenever an item gets worked on, that work will do all the processing relevant to that item (including some sort of re-adding if future processing is still desired).  If, subsequent to an item being worked on, that same items is worked on again later for some reason other than the last work requesting it, this is unnecessary work.

The lack of duplicate suppression between the FIFO and the timed delay part can lead to such unnecessary work.  Suppose that the item comes out of the FIFO and is worked on before it comes out of the timed delay.  In this case, when the item comes out of the timed delay, it is no longer in the FIFO so adding it there will not be suppressed.

This behavior was intentional. Imagine:

* T0: Item X begins processing.
* T1: Item X processor has read the state of X and begins a computation.
* T2: Item X changes again and is dirty.
* T3: Item X processor finishes its computation. (but it has not seen the most recent version of X)

It is necessary to re-process item X at this point. It's unavoidable because we don't know at what point in the processing the state of X was read.

I have been investigating the issue that @aojea mentioned above for the endpointslice controller https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/110642#issuecomment-1158909977.

What we are seeing is that because duplicates are not suppressed between the FIFO and the waiting queue, the controller doesn't respect the normal backoff period that it should since we are running out of retry budget because of Events on objects processed by the FIFO.

I understand the use-case you shared @lavalamp and I also think that suppressing the duplicates would break that exact scenario.

That said, I think that there might be something we could improve. Today, to respect the backoff period and the retry budget while still processing occasional events, the only solution I see is to have 2 queues, one handling all the events and the other taking care of retries and making sure to respect both the backoff period and the retry budget that is allocated. That's because today the only way to tell how many retries happened is to call [numRequeues](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/workqueue/default_rate_limiters.go#L110-L115), but as its name indicated it tells you how many items were queued but not how many were processed and whenever a controller calls [AddRateLimited](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/workqueue/rate_limiting_queue.go#L67-L70), it will increase the counter by one, so your budget runs out sooner than what you would expect. It gets even worst when Events are being processed by the FIFO and then on failure put into the waiting queue because your retry budget decrease faster than the actual number of retries you process. As such, would it make sense to embed a new counter inside of the rate-limited queue, that would keep track of the number of times a certain key has been moved from the delaying queue into the FIFO?
@dgrisonnet Please take a look at #112328 and see if that approach will solve this for you?
I completely missed that PR, thank you for sharing, I'll check it out.

@lavalamp : the scenario you outlined at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/110642#issuecomment-1230897214 involves only the FIFO and is not what this issue is about.  The FIFO has handled this correctly for years, see https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/release-1.20/util/workqueue/queue.go#L75-L77 .  Suppressing duplicates in the timed-delay part does not need to break this.  At first glance https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/112328 looks like it is de-duping in the way I would suggest (i.e., resolve the duplication by omitting the item from the time-delayed part, keeping it in the FIFO part).  (#112328 looks like it is making a bigger change than necessary to resolve just this issue.)

From what I understand the current implementation of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/112328 will cover both this issue with the preemptable queue behavior and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/112325 with the non-preemptable queue. The latter is similar to the issue I have outlined above in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/110642#issuecomment-1257921845 where rate limiting mechanisms aren't respected because events are directly added to the FIFO.

@lavalamp it seems that it isn't covering the behavior that I would want for the endpointslice controller.

In my case, I would want to keep the existing behavior with the duplicates where failures are being added to the waiting queue for retry, and events updating the state of the world are still being processed as soon as they arrive since they might resolve the issue at hand. But what I would need that doesn't exist yet is a counter of items that transitioned from the waiting queue to the FIFO in order to be able to tell where we are at in terms of retry budget. Since this is kind of different from the initial issue reported here, I can create another issue if you think that change would make sense.

> In my case, I would want to keep the existing behavior with the duplicates where failures are being added to the waiting queue for retry, and events updating the state of the world are still being processed as soon as they arrive since they might resolve the issue at hand. But what I would need that doesn't exist yet is a counter of items that transitioned from the waiting queue to the FIFO in order to be able to tell where we are at in terms of retry budget. Since this is kind of different from the initial issue reported here, I can create another issue if you think that change would make sense.

I 'm not sure that is the right approach, 
we have event X that fails to be reconciled, we retryAfter t secs
event X arrives directly , we know it failed that is why we retried, why do we want to process it immediately?

> event X arrives directly , we know it failed that is why we retried, why do we want to process it immediately?

If the event updates the state of the world, you don't know whether it will also fail or fix the issue causing the failures, so I am thinking that it might be better to treat it right away rather than wait for a delay that could reach a couple of minutes.
The benefit would be to be more reactive to changes fixing the state of the controller but at the cost of potentially continuing to process failures without waiting for the backoff delay.
then, how do you break the loop? assume worst case, that event reconciliation is always going to fail and the system will keep generating this event

It will be broken once you reach your retry budget, which is what we have in place today. The only difference is that today retry budgets only take into account additions to the waiting queue, so it tends to exhaust the budget way earlier than expected.
will not reset the retry budget every new event?

@dgrisonnet This is not a rate-limiting queue. I actually think what controllers need is a limited version of the priority and fairness algorithm. The point should be to fairly spend your limited amount of CPU/network on changes for well-behaved and poorly-behaved objects. Possibly with multiple priority levels... Hm, this sounds like fun to write

@MikeSpreitzer ah, I see what you are saying now, thanks. I'm not sure the linked issue resolves all aspects of it, I'll check for that during the next review pass.

I would expect `AddWithOptions(item, DelayingOptions{Duration: 0})` to behave the same as `AddAfter(item, 0)` or `Add(item)`. Any reason why not make it synchronous as well?

I wouldn't expect the two to work the same way for these reasons: -
* The new **WithOptions()** method makes synchronous/asynchronous an explicit option on the call and it would be confusing to mix explicit with implicit behaviour.
* Add/AddAfter can be viewed as the old interface, maintained for backwards compatibility, but AddWithOptions is intended to replace them.  Keeping the backwards compatibility allows us to keep the old behaviours that they provide, so that we don't need to refactor everything in one go but having the new interface (AddWithOptions) gives us a chance to expose the new different richer behaviour.
* With the new implementation there is now a performance penalty to making a synchronous add because it has to be processed though the waitLoop where it didn't before.  Unless you really need synchronous behaviour (in which case you can just ask for it in the options) then the default should be the more performant asynchronous add which returns back sooner and lets the client carry on with their work.

Could we also consider canceling/forgetting items functionality (https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/issues/131)?

As mentioned we are are using the delaying queue as a reminder in the controllers for availability check. We schedule the reminder when pod becomes `Ready` It would be great if we could cancel the reminder when the pod losts its readiness or gets deleted.

This feature request is not a must, but it would help the controller do less processing. Example of a usage https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/28e99532f83eeb2d69be56a0539951c687492ffa/pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go#L491 from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/113605.

I was unaware of this PR and opened mine which implements the forget https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/113607. I think it would be nice to have this as a part of this PR's API.

It is probably not a must at the moment, but wanted to bring awareness to this, and maybe we could add this in a followup?

This is why I implemented the Add() pre-empting the waiting item in the first place.  If you are going to queue an immediate processing of 'x' it does not make sense to keep the waiting 'x'.  Either the processing of 'x' is successful in which case the later check is superfluous and fine to be dropped, OR the processing fails (or it not in the desired state) and so a re-check is scheduled with an appropriate delay (i.e. we just checked it, we should back off before we testing/check/process it again).
AddAfter() already implements - bumping an item 'x' further up the waiting queue.

Ok, that makes in most scenarios. But it is not possible to cancel the processing altogether and to clean up the active/waiting queue. I agree, reconcilers should always proceed correctly regardless if the sync is needed or not, so it is not an issue of correctness, but just an optimization to do less processing.

Hi @atiratree

Thanks for the info on "stress".  I've run and found a race where it was possible for the clock to tick either to or past the time of the nextReady item.  In this scenario the nextReady channel will not fire.  I've been able to mitigate the race by placing a check for the nextReady item being ready directly before the select (and wait) and continue round the loop again, if there are ready items to pop.

In real life, outside of fake clocks and tests I would have expected this to have been rare and if it did happen then the heartbeat signal would have fired after 10 seconds, triggering the waitLoop to process the items again.
